doc.title: Dave Frishberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

title: How long a lyric takes: 'Blizzard of Lies' and 'Hershey Bar'
summary: A title can wait years; on deadline for Johnny Mandel he took four days, three of nothing, and finds pressure stimulating.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah. It’s unexpected I think and it really is a clever song too with all the kind of cliches of the language that we hear so often. How long does it take you on average to write a lyric like that?

That one took years. Not because it took years, because I carried the title around in my head for years before I ever acted on it. But I remember thinking that would be a great title. And then I never really followed through on it. I had it in mind for a decade though. But otherwise it depends. If I’m under the gun, and believe it or not there are situations even in today’s music business where I might be under the gun, like Johnny Mandel called me about a month ago before I came on this trip that I’m on now, and told me that he needed some material for a new record he was producing that was liable to be a popular record, and he told me he wanted me to write lyrics to his old song “Hershey Bar,” that Stan Getz record from 1948 or whatever. And he wanted it pretty quickly and promptly. So I rose to the occasion. I can still do it.

Although it’s tough for me to start, I’m a procrastinator. And I waited again until the last minute, but I got it in there. It took me three days, four days. But what it is is three days of nothing. And the fourth day of pouring forth. Without the three days of nothing, the fourth day was not going to happen. And that’s a horrible routine to have to get used to. I mean you might be a writer yourself, and you know how it feels to have nothing. But you’ve got to go through the nothing, trying again and again and again before the something will happen. That’s the hard part.
All the time you are saying yeah, yeah, it’s going to come, it’s going to come.
And the thing is, don’t stop, it’s okay. Yeah this does feel doomed but it’s not. Keep going you keep telling yourself.
That can be a little nerve wracking, especially if you have people waiting on you I suppose, or counting on you.
Well it can be nerve wracking and it can also be stimulating and it can be an impetus to your writing. It can make you write.
